newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Volvo pledges cuts, also eyes buys.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Volvo pledges cuts, also eyes buys.

text.p: Swedish vehicle maker AB Volvo pledged on Thursday to keep trimming costs while remaining on the lookout for possible acquisitions.

At a company seminar at Volvo's Gothenberg headquarters on Sweden's west coast, Volvo's new managing director Leif Johansson said the company was considering several business deals, including acquisitions.
"There are a number of business possibilities. It's natural for a company like Volvo to always have a shopping list of possible acquisitions," Johansson told reporters.
Johansson, who joined Volvo in April after heading appliance maker Electrolux, said Volvo's balance sheet was strong enough for an acquisition.

Volvo appeared to break out of a year-long downward trend in the fourth quarter of 1996, posting a better-than-expected nine percent rise in pre-tax profits for the year of 14.2 billion crowns. The first quarter 1997 continued this trend.

"I also think that our (5.2 billion crown) redemption programme has given us a relation to our shareholders that enables us to ask for more money if we find a unique business possibility," Johansson said.
Volvo's car division has so far been leading the upward trend, aided by a successful change from the 400 series to the S40/V40 models that has driven margins up.
Volvo Car's managing director Tuve Johannesson said the sales target of 100,000-110,000 S/V40 in 1997 would be reached.
However he said Volvo Car would continue to implement cuts in 1997 with costs per car estimated to fall by 5,000 crowns within the next 12 months.
"We will continue our focus on cost reductions," he said.
"We are looking to reduce costs at the same time as raising prices for our products. We are selling our models at a higher price which increases our profitability."
Johannesson also said Volvo would present an "exiting" new launch in the week of June 23 but gave no further details.
Volvo said other cost cuts would come by stepping up cooperation between various divisions within the company.
He said increased European integration would enable Volvo to concentrate operations at strategic locations, merging import and marketing companies for the different units.
Although eyeing new acquisitions, Johansson stressed that organic growth would be as important for the company.

"Over a period of time I think acquisitions and organic growth will be in balance," he said. "For Volvo, organic growth is most important. Acquisitions may be used to increase the product range, for example."
Acquisitions were a possibility for all divisions -- even for the troubled truck division whose sales slipped 13 percent last year mainly due to a poor performance in North America.
"The number one priority is internal control in North America and organic growth, but I cannot rule out an acquistion in North America," Johansson said.
In North America the picture was looking brighter with order intake rate rising more than 10 percent so far this year but operations were still posting a loss.
"We are still making a loss in North America but we see a continued and stable improvement," said Volvo Truck president Karl-Erling Trogen.
Volvo Trucks expected continued price pressure in Europe, particularly on the British and German markets where Mercedes was increasing its activities.
But Trogen said the European market was profitable and order intake strong so Volvo had increased its rate of manufacturing and was meeting competition by cutting costs.
Volvo shares closed 1.5 crowns higher at 209 crowns.
